opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's something we see play out constantly with the developers and companies we work with.

In the very early stage, when you're still figuring out product-market fit, speed of iteration is everything. You don't yet know what your users actually want, so you shouldn't be spending months fine-tuning or optimizing infrastructure. Most teams at that point reach for the biggest, most capable model available, often a closed frontier model through an API, because it lets them prototype quickly and validate whether the experience is even valuable. Quality is the bottleneck, not cost or latency.

But once you find product-market fit and usage starts to scale, the picture changes pretty dramatically. Suddenly you're looking at your inference bill growing faster than your revenue, or latency that's acceptable in a demo but frustrating for real users at volume. And you realize that you don't need a general-purpose model that can write poetry and solve olympiad math. You need a model that's really, really good at your specific task.

That's where we see a big shift toward smaller, open models that are customized, fine-tuned on your own data, maybe distilled from the larger model you started with. You get comparable or even better quality on your narrow use case, at a fraction of the cost and much lower latency. And importantly, you get control. You own the model, you can tune it, you're not subject to someone else changing the model underneath you.

Then in the more mature stage, it becomes about building a system rather than picking a single model. You might route different requests to different models, combine retrieval, tool use, multiple specialized components. It's what we call compound AI systems. The product's quality comes from how well those pieces are orchestrated and continuously improved with feedback from real usage.

So I'd summarize it as: early on, optimize for learning speed; at scale, optimize for quality, latency, and cost on your specific workload; and long term, optimize for control and continuous improvement. The model choice should evolve with the product, and the mistake we see is teams either over-engineering too early or staying locked into a one-size-fits-all model for too long.

r001.rationale: The response says teams initially use a powerful model because they do not yet know what users want, but it does not connect that uncertainty specifically to which product features will become established.

r002.rationale: It mentions validating whether an experience is valuable and improving from real usage, but does not say user responses identify which features are worth hardening.

r003.rationale: It connects a product’s specific, narrow task to customized smaller models that can perform well on that use case.

r004.rationale: It describes different model choices at successive stages and says choices should evolve, but does not clearly characterize the shift from the initial powerful model to a specialized model as gradual.

r005.rationale: It mentions fine-tuning on a team’s own data, but does not identify data accumulated through production use as the resource for tuning the model to the specific application.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about it as a journey, and the model choice really tracks where you are on that journey. In the very beginning, when you're still figuring out whether there's even a product here, you want the most capable model you can get your hands on, period. You're not optimizing for cost, you're not optimizing for latency, you're optimizing for signal. You want to know: does this idea work at all? Can the model do the thing? So you reach for the frontier, you prototype fast, you iterate on prompts, and you don't worry about the economics yet.

Then something shifts once you have product-market fit. Suddenly you have real traffic, you have users who care about response time, and the bill from that frontier model starts to look pretty scary. That's when the conversation changes from "can this work" to "can this work at scale." And at that point, you start looking at smaller models, open models, models you can fine-tune on your own data. Because by then you actually have data. You have thousands or millions of real interactions that tell you what your users want, and that's incredibly valuable. A smaller model that's been tuned on your specific task will very often match or beat the big general model on that task, at a fraction of the cost and latency.

And then there's a third stage, where you're mature, you're at scale, and you start decomposing the problem. You realize you don't need one model doing everything. You have a routing layer, you have specialized models for different sub-tasks, maybe a bigger model handling the hard cases and a tiny one handling the easy ninety percent. That's where you get the real step-function improvements in quality and efficiency.

So the way I'd summarize it: early on, buy capability. In the middle, buy control. At scale, buy composability. The mistake I see most often is teams trying to optimize cost before they've proven the product, or conversely, teams that never leave the frontier model even when they have everything they need to move off it.

r001.rationale: The response says that early on, while the team is still figuring out whether a product will work, it should use the most capable model to learn what is possible.

r002.rationale: It says real interactions reveal what users want, but does not connect observed responses to identifying which specific features are worth hardening.

r003.rationale: It recommends specialized models for different subtasks at maturity, but does not tie that choice to established product features having narrower problem definitions.

r004.rationale: The response presents distinct early, middle, and mature stages, but does not describe the shift from a powerful initial model to a specialized model as gradual.

r005.rationale: It says production interactions provide data that can be used to fine-tune smaller models for the product's specific task.

astra-6.text:
I think it starts with what you’re trying to learn at that stage. When you’re building a prototype, the biggest question is often, does this product solve a real problem? You want to move quickly, so starting with a capable general-purpose model through an API can make sense. You don’t necessarily want to invest in customizing a model before you’ve validated the use case.

As the product matures, you understand your workload much better. You know where the model makes mistakes, what latency users will tolerate, and what each interaction costs. Then you can make a more informed choice: perhaps a smaller model is sufficient, perhaps you need fine-tuning, or perhaps you route different tasks to different models.

So I wouldn’t treat model selection as a decision you make once. Early on, you’re optimizing for learning and iteration. As you scale, you’re increasingly optimizing for reliable quality, latency, and cost on the specific tasks your users care about.

r001.rationale: The response recommends a capable general-purpose model for prototyping, but does not connect that choice to uncertainty about which product features will become established.

r002.rationale: It does not say that observed user responses identify which features are worth hardening.

r003.rationale: It mentions specific tasks and options such as fine-tuning or routing, but does not connect established features’ narrower problem definitions to specialized models.

r004.rationale: It describes model choices changing as a product matures, but does not describe a gradual shift from a powerful initial model to a specialized model.

r005.rationale: It does not identify data accumulated through production use as a resource for tuning a model to the product’s application.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the stage of the product makes a big difference. Early on, you’re trying to figure out whether you’re solving the right problem. You want to iterate quickly, so starting with a capable, general-purpose model often makes sense. You can establish what a good experience looks like before investing heavily in optimization.

As the product matures, you learn which tasks actually matter, where the model fails, and what your users expect. Then you can make more deliberate choices: perhaps a smaller model is sufficient, perhaps you need fine-tuning, or perhaps different parts of the application should use different models.

At scale, cost, latency, and reliability become much more significant. The question becomes, ‘Which model meets the quality requirement for this particular task at the right operational cost?’ And you need evaluations grounded in your product to answer that. The model choice should evolve as your understanding of the product evolves.
